III p312.text: One attains, then, to a representation of moral freedom, only through the most lively representation of suffering nature: and the tragic hero must legitimate himself in our opinion as a susceptible being, before we can do homage to him as a rational being, and believe in his strength of spirit.
III p312.alignment: One complete sentence: the vivid representation of suffering nature precedes recognition of the tragic hero as a rational being. Weiss preserves the German argument and order.

III p345.text:
All emotions are more æsthetic at second hand, and no sympathy is stronger than that which we feel with sympathy.

Post ipsum auxilio subeuntem ac tela ferentem
Corripiunt.
III p345.alignment: The English sentence preserves the claims that emotions are more aesthetic at second hand and sympathy with sympathy is strongest. The following excerpt of Virgil, Aeneid II.216–217, remains in Latin, untranslated; Weiss prints it as a separate two-line block after a full stop, where the German connects it with a comma. The Latin excerpt is the same, including its incomplete final verse.

III p312.alignment: Personally read German 1801 p. 312 and Weiss 1845 p. 202: one complete sentence, freedom through vivid suffering nature, the tragic hero as a feeling being before the rational being and strength of spirit. The split word and colon spacing corrections match print.
